673.title: Faith and works (James 2:14–26)
673.hook: faith without works is dead; Luther found James hard, but all churches read it
673.howItsDone: Christians read James 2 alongside Paul's letters, and churches often pair Sunday worship with practical service, such as food banks, coat drives and visiting, as faith put to work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gold ring and a good seat, and your line was mercy triumphs over judgment.

It's winter. A neighbor knocks on your door. No coat, and they haven't eaten since yesterday. You smile warmly and say, I'll be thinking of you. Stay warm. Eat something. Then you close the door. James paints this scene and asks: what good is that? It's the setup for a paragraph Christians still argue over. Martin Luther found it hard going. And still, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles all keep it.

In the King James Bible: "If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?" Then: "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." A faith that only talks is like those warm words at the door: it sounds right and changes nothing. James gets sharp: you believe there is one God? Good. "The devils also believe, and tremble." Knowing the right facts isn't the same as trusting with your life. Then two examples. Abraham, willing to offer Isaac. And Rahab, the woman in Jericho who hid Israel's spies and sent them out another way. A patriarch and an outsider. Faith showed itself in what each did. "For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also." Why the argument? Paul wrote that a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law. James writes that a person is justified by works, and not by faith only. In his 1522 preface to the New Testament, Martin Luther called James a letter of straw, compared with books like Romans. He still kept it in his Bible. Christians read the two side by side differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often point to James when they teach that God's grace saves through a faith alive with love and good works. Protestant churches in Luther's line teach that people are saved by faith alone, and that real faith always gets up and does something, which is how they read James. James's own point is plain: a faith that never opens the door isn't what he means by faith.
screen: then, large: `FAITH, IF IT HATH NOT WORKS, IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: Think of one need you know about right now, one person: a neighbor, a coworker. Picture the warm words you might say, then one thing your hands could actually do, out of faith or simply out of love: a meal, a ride, a call. If you pray, ask for the courage to follow through.
Works. James's test for living faith: faith without works is dead, the same way a body without breath is dead.
Your line: faith that works. Warm words, and an open door. See you tomorrow.

674.title: The tongue (James 3:1–12)
674.hook: a small rudder, a small spark: the tongue sets forests on fire
674.howItsDone: Some Christians include their speech in a daily or weekly self-examination, and churches turn to James 3 when teaching about gossip, anger and online behavior.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith and works, warm words at a closed door, and your line was faith that works.

A wildfire can start from almost nothing. A spark from a dragged chain. One cigarette. A campfire left smoldering. A few days later the smoke is visible from space, and whole towns are packing their cars. Investigators sometimes trace the fire back to a single point on the ground, small enough to cover with your hand. James never saw a satellite photo, but he knew what a small fire can do, and he used it to describe something that sits in every mouth.

He starts with a warning to teachers. Not many of you should become teachers, he says, because teachers will be judged more strictly. People who talk for a living have more to answer for. Then three pictures of small things steering big ones. A bit in a horse's mouth turns the whole animal. A huge ship, driven by fierce winds, is "turned about with a very small helm," the rudder, wherever the pilot wants. And then: "Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!" That word matter is a puzzle in English. The Greek word means wood, or forest. How great a forest a small fire sets ablaze. The bit and the rudder steer. The spark destroys. Then something that stings: people have tamed every kind of animal, birds and snakes and sea creatures, "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison." And the line that turns it inward: "Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be." With the tongue, James says, we bless God, and with it we curse people made in God's likeness. Praise on Sunday, cursing by Monday. Does a spring pour fresh water and bitter from the same opening? Can a fig tree grow olives? He isn't saying never speak. He's saying words are fire. They can warm a house or burn it down, and the same mouth does both.
screen: then, large: `HOW GREAT A MATTER A LITTLE FIRE KINDLETH!`

segments.voice: Think back to the last unkind thing you said, out loud or in a text, and without punishing yourself, picture it like a spark landing in dry grass. Then picture the moment today you're most likely to say something sharp, and your mouth staying closed, or opening with something else after a breath. If you pray, you can ask for a guard on your mouth.
The tongue. For James, a small part of the body that steers like a rudder and burns like a spark, and that no one can fully tame.
Your line: a small fire. One spark, one forest. Day six hundred seventy-four, done.

675.title: Wisdom from above (James 3:13–18)
675.hook: peaceable, gentle, easy to entreat, full of mercy
675.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to James 3:17 as a short list of what wise leadership looks like, and some churches use it when choosing leaders or working through a dispute.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tongue, a little fire, and your line was a small fire.

Who is the wisest person you know? Not the smartest. Not the one with the most degrees or the quickest comeback. The wisest. Maybe you're picturing someone calm. Someone you could tell anything to, who listens before answering and leaves the room more peaceful than they found it. Cleverness wins arguments. Wisdom often looks gentler. James asks the question straight out: who is wise among you? Then he describes two kinds of wisdom.

First, the test. If you're wise, James says, show it by a good life, by works done in "meekness of wisdom." Meekness isn't weakness. It's strength that doesn't need to shove. Then the first kind of wisdom, the kind from below: full of bitter envy and selfish ambition. It may look clever. It may even win. But James is blunt about what it leaves behind: "For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work." Confusion is disorder, things coming apart, like an office run on rivalry or a family where everyone keeps score. Then the second kind. In the King James Bible: "But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy." Seven marks, and not one is about being clever. Pure, with no hidden motive. Peaceable. Gentle, a word that means reasonable, yielding. Easy to be intreated, one word in Greek, which as far as we know appears only here in the New Testament: open to persuasion, willing to change your mind. Full of mercy. Without partiality, an echo of James's gold ring. Without hypocrisy, the same inside as outside. And he closes with a seed: "And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace." Peacemakers plant, and what grows is goodness. Wisdom from above isn't measured by how hard you win. It's measured by what grows after you leave.
screen: then, large: `THE WISDOM THAT IS FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Remember the last time someone disagreed with you or tried to correct you, and how your body reacted: a tight jaw, crossed arms, a reply already loading. Now picture the same moment, easy to be intreated: shoulders down, asking tell me more, letting them finish, allowing that they might be right. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom from above.
Meekness. James's word for strength that doesn't need to shove: wisdom from above, pure, peaceable, gentle, open to persuasion, full of mercy.
Your line: gentle wisdom. Strength that doesn't need to shove. Until tomorrow, then.

676.title: Draw near to God (James 4:1–10)
676.hook: draw near to God and he will draw near to you
676.howItsDone: Some churches use James 4:8 as a call to worship or before a prayer of confession, especially in Lent, when worshipers are invited to come near to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wisdom from above, gentle and easy to be intreated, and your line was gentle wisdom.

"From whence come wars and fightings among you?" That's how James opens chapter four, in the King James Bible, and he isn't talking about armies. He means the believers he's writing to. Arguments in the parking lot. Grudges that last for years. Where does all that come from? It's a fair question for any family, any office, any group chat that's gone quiet and cold. James's answer is uncomfortable, and then, a few lines later, it turns into a promise.

Here's his answer: "come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" The fight outside starts as a fight inside. You want something and don't have it, so you scheme and quarrel. Then a short line that stings: "ye have not, because ye ask not." Or you ask with the wrong motives, just to spend it on your own pleasures. Then James quotes Proverbs: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." And the letter turns. A string of short commands, almost like a drumbeat. "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you." Some readers hear a priestly word in draw nigh: the old Greek translation of Exodus uses it for priests who come near to the Lord. If so, James hands that priestly word to everyone. And the promise has two sides. You take a step, and God takes a step. In James's picture, God isn't waiting at a distance with crossed arms. God comes toward you. Then what drawing near looks like: wash your hands, purify your hearts, you double minded. Let your laughter turn to mourning, he says, meaning take your wrongs seriously. Then the last line lifts everything back up: "Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up." The fights start inside, and so does the way back.
screen: `YE HAVE NOT, BECAUSE YE ASK NOT.`

segments.voice: Picture a doorway, and you standing a few steps back from it, and name what has kept you at a distance lately: busyness, a quarrel, shame, or just forgetting. In your mind, take one step forward, toward God or toward the holy as you understand it, without fixing everything first, and imagine the other side of the promise: the doorway coming closer to you too. If you pray, you can simply say, here I am.
Double minded. James's name for the proud and quarreling: told to purify their hearts and draw near to God, who then draws near to them.
Your line: draw near. A promise with two sides. That's day six hundred seventy-six.

677.title: If the Lord wills (James 4:11–17)
677.hook: you are a mist that appears for a little while
677.howItsDone: Some Christians add "God willing" or "Lord willing" when speaking of future plans, and some still write D.V., for Deo volente, at the end of a letter or a notice of meetings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a promise with two sides, draw near to God, and your line was draw near.

Open your calendar app. Look at next month, laid out in neat colored blocks: the trip, the deadline, the dentist, the dinner. It looks so certain on the screen. Now think back to a year ago. How much of what you planned then happened the way you planned it? James turns to people making plans like that: traders off to a city for a year to buy and sell. And he sounds like he's reading over their shoulder.

First a quick word against speaking evil of one another: there is one judge, he says, so who are you to judge your neighbor? Then the business plan. In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain." Very specific, and very confident. Then James says: "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." A vapor. The breath you see on a cold morning. The steam off a cup of coffee. The mist on a field at dawn that's gone by nine. It's real, and then it isn't. James doesn't say, so don't plan. He gives better words for planning: "For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that." Make the plan. Hold it with an open hand. The phrase passed into Christian speech. Some still write the Latin letters D.V., Deo volente, God willing, at the bottom of a letter about future plans. Muslims say something close, in sha' Allah, if God wills, and Jews say im yirtzeh Hashem. It's a shared human humility about tomorrow. And the passage ends with a line that turns it around: "Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin." If life is a vapor, the good you know you could do is for today. Not someday.

Picture your plans for the rest of today and tomorrow, each one written on a little card, held in an open hand instead of a fist, and notice which one you're gripping hardest. Breathe out slowly and watch the breath disappear, the way James's vapor does. If you pray, you can offer your plans to God.
Vapor. James's picture for a life that's here today and gone tomorrow: the breath you see on a cold morning, real, and then gone.
Your line: a little while. Plans in an open hand. See you tomorrow.

678.title: Wages held back (James 5:1–6)
678.hook: the wages you withheld cry out
678.howItsDone: Some churches draw on James 5 and Deuteronomy 24 in their teaching on fair wages and workers' rights, and some congregations make a point of paying their own staff and contractors promptly and fairly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a life like vapor, and your line was a little while.

Sundown at the edge of a harvested field. The reapers have been cutting grain since morning, and now they wait for the day's pay. No savings account. No paycheck next Friday. The old law of Moses says why that pay can't wait: the worker is poor, and has set his heart on it. Tonight the owner says, come back next week. That's the scene behind today's passage. And James, practical and plainspoken for four chapters, suddenly raises his voice.

In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you." It sounds like the old prophets, Amos or Isaiah, thundering against injustice. Then pictures of wealth rotting where it's stored: "Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten." The gold and silver, he says, have rusted, and the rust will be a witness against you. Hoarded things decay. Then the heart of it: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth." The wages themselves cry out. Money that should have been in a worker's hand has a voice, and it reaches God. Deuteronomy says to pay a poor laborer his wage on the same day, before the sun goes down, so that he doesn't cry to the Lord against you. James is drawing on that old command. And notice the title he uses for God. Lord of sabaoth. It isn't sabbath. It's a Hebrew word meaning armies, or hosts. The Lord of hosts. The commander of heaven's armies is listening to the cry of a farmhand who wasn't paid. Some churches teach from this passage that a fair wage, paid on time, isn't charity. It's justice.
screen: then, large: `KEPT BACK BY FRAUD, CRIETH.`

segments.voice: Think of the people whose work you depend on and rarely see: the person who picks your fruit, who cleans the office at night, who sews the clothes you're wearing. Then think closer to home: do you owe anyone right now, a babysitter, a friend who covered lunch, a bill you've let slide? If you pray, you can pray for workers who are waiting on wages.
Sabaoth. Hebrew for hosts, armies, the Lord of hosts: the title James uses when he says a worker's unpaid wages cry out and reach God's ears.
Your line: the wages cry out. And the Lord of hosts hears. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

679.title: The patient farmer (James 5:7–12)
679.hook: the farmer waits for the early and late rain
679.howItsDone: James 5:7–10 is an Advent reading in some church lectionaries, in the season of waiting before Christmas, and Christians often turn to it in long illnesses or hard seasons.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wages held back, and sabaoth, the Lord of hosts who hears the unpaid. Your line was the wages cry out.

You can't make a seed grow faster by yelling at it. You plant, you water, and then you wait, and the waiting is most of the work. The Bible speaks of two rains in that land, the early rain and the latter rain. Commentators place the early one in autumn, softening hard ground for plowing and sowing, and the latter in spring, swelling the grain before harvest. Between them, months of watching the sky. James has just thundered at the rich who cheated their workers. Now he turns to his brethren, people waiting for things to be put right, and gives them a farmer to look at.

In the King James Bible: "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain." Husbandman is the old word for farmer. And his patience isn't idle. Farmers weed, mend fences and fix the plow, but they can't make it rain. Be patient like that, James says, and steady your hearts, because the coming of the Lord is near. Then a warning for people under strain: "Grudge not one against another." Long waiting turns people on each other. Look, the judge is standing at the door. Then two more pictures of endurance. The prophets, who spoke for God and suffered for it. And: "Ye have heard of the patience of Job." Patient as Job, people say. Yet in the book of Job, he doesn't sit quietly. He argues, laments and demands an answer from God. The Greek word James uses here means endurance, staying under the weight, and that is exactly what Job did: he complained loudly, and he didn't let go. You've seen how it ended, James says: the Lord is full of pity and mercy. Last, a word about honesty: don't swear oaths. "Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay."
